{{Short description|Method for reconstructing a harmonic function in a domain}}
{{About|the method in mathematics|the hair painting technique|Hair highlighting#Hair painting}} 
In [[potential theory]], a mathematical discipline, '''balayage''' (from French: ''[[wiktionary:fr:balayage|balayage]]'' "scanning, sweeping") is a method devised by [[Henri Poincaré]] for reconstructing an [[harmonic function]] in a domain from its values on the boundary of the domain.<ref>{{SpringerEOM| title=Balayage method | id=Balayage_method | oldid=11819 | first=E.D. | last=Solomentsev }}</ref>

In modern terms, the '''balayage operator''' maps a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] <math>\mu</math> on a closed domain <math>D</math> to a measure <math>\nu</math> on the boundary <math>\part D</math>, so that the [[Newtonian potential]]s of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> coincide outside <math>\bar D</math>. The procedure is called balayage since the mass is "swept out" from <math>D</math> onto the boundary.

For <math>x</math> in <math>D</math>, the balayage of [[Dirac delta function|<math>\delta_x</math>]] yields the [[harmonic measure]] <math>\nu_x</math> corresponding to <math>x</math>. Then the value of a harmonic function <math>f</math> at <math>x</math> is equal to<math display="block"> f(x) = \int_{\partial D} f(y) \, d\nu_x(y).</math>

== Examples ==
[[File:VFPt_imagecharge_plane_horizontal_plusminus.svg|right|thumb|The field of a positive charge above a flat conducting surface, found by the method of images.]]
In gravity, [[Shell theorem|Newton's shell theorem]] is an example. Consider a uniform mass distribution within a solid ball <math>B</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.  The balayage of this mass distribution onto the surface of the ball (a sphere, <math>\partial B</math>) results in a uniform surface mass density.  The gravitational potential outside the ball is identical for both the original solid ball and the swept-out surface mass.

In electrostatics, the [[method of image charges]] is an example of "reverse" balayage. Consider a point charge <math>q</math> located at a distance <math>d</math> from an infinite, grounded conducting plane. The effect of the charges on the conducting plane can be "reverse balayaged" to a single "image charge" of <math>-q</math> at the mirror image position with respect to the plane.
